---
title: "A lever without a pill: the vagus and the locus coeruleus"
description: "Transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation may reach the brain's norepinephrine centre — a non-drug way to test the system."
author: "Yannick Loth"
date: "2026-09-20"
categories: [Arousal system, Noradrenergic, Mechanisms]
---

If the problem is a shortage of central norepinephrine, one obvious question is whether you can raise it without a drug. There is a plausible route: the vagus nerve.

Vagal afferents carry signals from the body to the brainstem nucleus of the solitary tract, which projects to the **locus coeruleus** — the brain's main norepinephrine nucleus. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) applies a small electrical signal to the ear, and reviews describe it as activating this locus-coeruleus-norepinephrine pathway (@Hilz2022taVNS). In mice, taVNS activated norepinephrine-producing (tyrosine-hydroxylase-positive) neurons in the locus coeruleus, and those neurons mediated the treatment's effects (@Lv2024taVNSLC).

**Why this is attractive.** Unlike stimulants, taVNS does not push the system with a drug, is reversible, and can be dose-controlled. If it works, it is also a **probe**: a safe way to test whether raising norepinephrine changes anything measurable.

**The limits.** The human evidence is at review level; the direct mechanistic evidence is in mice; and ME/CFS-specific data are preliminary. And a key caveat runs through the whole series: the underlying deficit itself is unreplicated.

**How we would know.** A trial could ask whether taVNS changes a non-invasive norepinephrine readout — pupil measures, handgrip endurance, a urine ratio — and, if the clearance loop is real, whether it changes a clearance or inflammatory marker. If it moves nothing, the non-drug route is unlikely to matter.

*Not a recommendation — a testable idea.*
